comments.text:
In regards to the conversation at the end, I was poor and got a 1340 out of 1600 SAT score. I only missed one question on the language and logic section and got my butt kicked by the math section. I was an AP scholar with honors. My dad stopped working for health reasons when I was 12 and had a stroke on my 18th birthday and we started taling care of him for the next 12 years. These days I'm working part time in a pizza place. I'm sure poverty disadvantages a lot of people academically, but I also think a lot of scholastic success is determined by inspiring a love of learning in a child/person and fostering a culture that values education and expertise. I think, for a lot of poor folks, the usefulness of education seems like an abstract concept, and it doesn't help that this country has a long running anti-intellectual streak. I say this of course realizing the deleterious effect that not having things like your own transportation or a quiet place to study can have on a person. I was lucky enough to have at least those things.

Now did I add up to much despite that success or talent in school? No. And that's a different matter to consider, how lots of seemingly bright kids become burn outs, and what might be done to prevent that, but let's stick to the one topic for now.
